blocks.text: 1. Security
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060456-119060059.png
Security, protecting a RAG system's data, prompts, and access from misuse, broadens the safety concerns raised elsewhere in this course into a dedicated, systemic discipline.
It treats every input from outside the system as potentially adversarial, not just as ordinary data.
2. Security Spans More Than Just Guardrails
Guardrails covered how to keep a single conversation on topic and safe.
Security broadens that concern to data protection, access control, and the whole system's attack surface.

blocks.text: 3. Prompt Injection From Retrieved Content
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060782-487837467.png
A malicious document injected into the knowledge base can carry hidden instructions for the model, similar to the instruction-override risk that guardrails address for direct prompts.
Retrieval itself becomes an attack surface, not just the user's direct query.
4. Data Leakage Through Generated Answers
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060782-705046158.png
A generated answer can accidentally reveal sensitive content it was never meant to surface, the same risk seen when an answer references a specific user's account details in Response Cache.
The generation step itself needs its own leak prevention, not just the retrieval step.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A generated summary that unintentionally includes a snippet from a document the current user was never permitted to see is a real leak, even if retrieval itself was working correctly.

blocks.text: 5. Access Control At The Retrieval Level

blocks.alt: Access Control At The Retrieval Level
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060782-98159649.png
A user should only ever retrieve chunks their own permissions actually allow, the same principle behind metadata filtering in Vector Databases.
Permission checks need to happen before retrieval, not just before showing the final answer.
6. Securing Infrastructure Beyond The RAG Pipeline Itself

blocks.alt: Securing Infrastructure Beyond The RAG Pipeline Itself
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060783-560297624.png
The vector database, cache, and logs are each real infrastructure with their own security surface, the same storage that Embedding Cache covered at scale.
Securing the RAG logic alone is not enough if the underlying storage itself is left exposed.

blocks.text: 7. Audit Logs For Security Incidents
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060783-171304910.png
Investigating a suspected security incident requires records of exactly who accessed what and when, the same correlation IDs that link logs across stages in Logging.
That same structured logging doubles as a security audit trail.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: The same structured, correlated logging covered in Logging provides exactly the who-accessed-what-and-when trail an investigator needs after a suspected security incident, without requiring a separate logging system.

blocks.text: 8. Security Adds Friction By Design
Every additional security check adds a validation step before something is allowed to proceed, much like validating triples against the schema in Graph Construction.
Security trades some convenience and latency for protection against real misuse.
9. Recognizing When A Dedicated Security Layer Earns Its Added Friction

blocks.alt: Recognizing When A Dedicated Security Layer Earns Its Added Friction
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060783-480793819.png
A system handling sensitive or permissioned data needs a dedicated security layer.
A system serving only public, non-sensitive information needs lighter security controls instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates permission-filtered retrieval and a check for leaked content in the generated answer.

code.content:
documents = [
    {"id": "d1", "text": "The Falcon plan costs twenty dollars per month.", "allowed_roles": ["public"]},
    {"id": "d2", "text": "Internal margin on the Falcon plan is five dollars.", "allowed_roles": ["admin"]},
]

def permission_filtered_retrieve(query, user_role):
    # access control at the retrieval level
    return [doc for doc in documents if user_role in doc["allowed_roles"]]

def generate_answer(retrieved_docs):
    return " ".join(doc["text"] for doc in retrieved_docs)

def check_for_leak(answer, restricted_terms):
    # checking for data leakage in the generated answer
    return [term for term in restricted_terms if term in answer.lower()]

user_role = "public"
retrieved = permission_filtered_retrieve("What does the Falcon plan cost?", user_role)
print(f"Retrieved for role '{user_role}':")
for doc in retrieved:
    print(f"  {doc['id']}: {doc['text']}")

answer = generate_answer(retrieved)
leaks = check_for_leak(answer, ["margin"])
print(f"\nGenerated answer: {answer}")
print(f"Leak check result: {'CLEAN' if not leaks else 'LEAK DETECTED: ' + str(leaks)}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the public role never even retrieving the internal margin document, keeping the generated answer clean by construction. This is why retrieval-level access control is the right place for the permission check.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Filtering permissions only after generation instead of at the retrieval step itself.
Treating retrieved documents as inherently trustworthy instead of a real attack surface.
Securing the RAG pipeline logic while leaving the underlying vector database or logs exposed.
Skipping structured, correlated logging that would otherwise double as a security audit trail.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Security protects a RAG system's data, prompts, and access from misuse.
It broadens guardrails' single-conversation focus to data protection and the whole attack surface.
A malicious document in the knowledge base can carry hidden instructions, making retrieval an attack surface.
A generated answer can leak sensitive content even when retrieval itself worked correctly.
Permission checks belong at the retrieval level, before a chunk ever reaches the model.
The vector database, cache, and logs are each real infrastructure with their own security surface.
Structured, correlated logging doubles as an audit trail for investigating security incidents.
Every additional security check trades some convenience and latency for protection against misuse.
